items.title: DeepInfer: High-performance inference framework for DeepSeek models
items.content:
DeepInfer is the high-performance inference framework that powers DeepSeek's large-scale production services. This open-source release provides offline inference with the core features needed for serving at scale.

Optimized kernels, model and sampler runtime

Parallelism: Attention DP / balanced CP, MoE EP + EPLB

DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification

Asynchronous scheduling (zero-overhead batch scheduler)

Optimized kernels: FlashMLA , DeepGEMM , DeepEP , TileKernels , DeepSelect , and custom TileLang kernels .

DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification: accelerate decoding with draft tokens and use confidence estimates to schedule verification. Set DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=1 ; DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE controls the maximum draft length (default: 5).

Decoder SWA bounded replay: reduce decoder prefill work by replaying only a bounded suffix. Set DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE=compact and DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140 for the default V4.1 settings; the retained suffix must cover the SWA window plus the maximum backtracking length.

Asynchronous scheduling: overlap CPU batch scheduling with device execution. Enabled by default.

Batch-invariant inference: keep model results identical across different batch compositions. Enable with DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 (NVIDIA only).

Deterministic sampling: produce identical outputs for identical input tokens and sampling parameters. Set DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0 and pass a fixed seq_seed to SamplingParams (NVIDIA only).

Structured outputs: constrain generation to a regex, JSON schema, or EBNF grammar. Pass so_args={"schema_type": ..., "schema": ...} to SamplingParams ; see examples .

Required for a complete inference service (not included in this release):

VE/Prefill/Decode disaggregation (most required engine functionality is already implemented)

Load balancing across data-parallel replicas for both prefill and decode

Before building DeepInfer, please create and activate an empty Python 3.12 environment.

# Use `ascend` instead for the Ascend platform

# Keep it exported in the environment where you run DeepInfer

The default checkpoint, deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 , is

downloaded into the Hugging Face cache on the first run; set DEEPINFER_HF_MODEL_DIR=/path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 to

Measured on 4 SM100 GPUs for prefill and 64 for decode — each within one scale-up domain. To reproduce the benchmarks, see run_sweep.sh .

DeepInfer is released under the Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE for details.

DeepInfer was originally built primarily on vLLM , with additional inspiration from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM . We thank their developers.

NorthPoint Development, a company seeking to build a data center campus in Hazle Township, a rural community in the Poconos, has offered to write $10,000 checks to about 4,500 households in exchange for their support of the project. Above, a data center owned by Lightedge is shown in Altoona, Iowa.

Residents of a small community in the Poconos are being enticed with the offer of a $10,000 payment — no strings attached — to throw their support behind a developer's plan for a massive data center campus that has faced staunch opposition in Luzerne County.

NorthPoint Development, a Missouri company that specializes in large-scale industrial projects, wants to construct up to 15 data center buildings in the foothill community of Hazle Township. The proposal would cover about 1,300 acres.

When local officials rejected the project last fall, citing zoning restrictions, NorthPoint sued to overturn the decision , but lost the case. The township then enacted a six-month moratorium on data center applications, sending NorthPoint back to the drawing board while officials update local zoning laws. The moratorium ends in January.

The Wall Street Journal reported Sunday that Hazle residents began receiving letters in the mail from NorthPoint in June. The company is willing to pay $10,000 to each of the township's roughly 4,500 households if leaders in Hazle approve the project. That equates to a $45 million fund to buy local support, and the letter from the developer said residents could use the money for "whatever you want."

Despite the temptation to take a check, the strategy does not appear to be swaying a large number of Hazle residents. Many are worried about the raft of issues that have led communities across the country to spurn data center projects. In addition to fears about heavy water usage, noise and upward pressure on energy costs, homeowners are wary of how a data center will affect the value of their properties.

“$10,000 doesn’t match how much it’s going to tank my property value,” Jeff Fasnacht, a retired teacher who lives near the proposed site of NorthPoint's data center, told the Wall Street Journal.

Limited research on how data centers affect home values has been mixed. The National Association of Realtors released a study this month showing dramatic differences across markets where campuses have been built during the rush to power AI development. Despite the pace of data center growth and their growing importance in the sphere of politics, NAR found they're concentrated in areas that make up about 1% of the country.

Counties with more data centers tend to have higher home values, higher incomes and better long-term job growth than those without them, the study found, backing other research showing greater benefits of such facilities for already-wealthy communities. Home values in counties with high concentrations of data centers — meaning 10 or more — have grown about 95% over the past decade, compared to 64% growth in counties without data centers.

But at a more local level, the effect of data centers is too varied to generalize.

"We do not see evidence of weaker housing markets in counties with a large data center presence,” NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement accompanying the study. “But these are county-level numbers, and they can’t tell us what happens to an individual home next to a facility. That’s why local knowledge and credible data matter so much right now.”

In Hazle, where the median household income is $60,000, taking a $10,000 check from NorthPoint could be a considerable financial help to many residents. Most of those interviewed by the Wall Street Journal said they recognize what the money would do for them, but still would prefer not have a data center in town.

Data center developers have increasingly touted community benefits agreements to gain the support of local governments, promising long-term funding for essential services…

items.content:
The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores.

To demonstrate that the keys are compromised, the original reporter Wayne signed the following message with the private key of each of the eight intermediate CAs and reported it to the Root Program Teams on the 17th of October:

proof.zip contains the message, and for each intermediate the certificate, its public key and a signature on the message. To verify with OpenSSL:

The root programs and many downstream trust stores have taken action to protect their users. The certificates have been blocked in Firefox and Chrome since the 17th of October and in Apple devices since the 19th.

The issue was responsibly disclosed to downstream trust stores on the 19th of October. Many have already released updates or are in the process of releasing updates.

An attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs could impersonate any website or service.

This has already been remediated by Mozilla, Apple and Chrome for their users through their tools for distributing revocation information such as OneCRL , CRLite and CRLSets .

The CA has also revoked the compromised intermediate certificates. However, many other clients do not consume revocation information and require software updates to ensure they no longer trust the compromised intermediates.

To check curl or other command-line clients, run:

A certificate error means the client does not trust the compromised intermediates.

To check a trust store offline, chains.zip contains the certificate chain served by each of the twelve hosts above in PEM format, with instructions for verifying them with OpenSSL.

impacted-intermediates.json lists the eight intermediates and their Sectigo cross-signs. roots.json lists the roots they chain to.

The private keys for the intermediate certificates were incorrectly generated by the CA. This means that anyone can recover them from the certificates.

This would have been possible since the certificates were created in April 2025. There are no entries in the certificate transparency logs for these intermediates in that period, indicating that CT-enforcing clients like Firefox, Chrome, Edge and Safari could not have been attacked.

However, many clients outside of the browser ecosystem do not enforce Certificate Transparency. We do not know if attackers exploited the flawed key generation to target these clients.

Further technical information about the cause is captured in the initial incident report in Mozilla's bug tracker.

Please see this thread in Mozilla's dev-security-policy forum.

Users should update their browsers and operating systems to the latest versions as soon as possible.

items.title: Protecting Firefox users following the compromise of eMudhra intermediate certificates
items.content:
On Saturday, October 17, at 20:06 UTC, Mozilla received a report that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates had been compromised. These keys could allow attackers to issue fraudulent HTTPS certificates for websites they do not control. An attacker who could intercept a user’s connection could use those certificates to impersonate websites and potentially read or modify traffic.

Mozilla engineers responded immediately, blocking the affected certificates in Firefox using OneCRL , Mozilla’s centralized list of revoked certificates. OneCRL delivers this protection without requiring users to update or restart Firefox.

By 22:59 UTC that same day, in less than 3 hours after we received the report, the updated OneCRL distribution was complete for all Firefox users with standard configurations.

Today, we are also releasing Firefox 158.0.1 for Desktop and Android, along with Firefox ESR 115.43.1 and Firefox ESR 153.5.1 . These releases will distribute this protection for a minority of users whose custom settings may have prevented them from receiving the OneCRL update.

We are also updating the trusted certificate list in NSS ( NSS 3.131.1 ) to remove the root certificate that signed the affected intermediates. Firefox is already protected through OneCRL, but this additional update helps protect other applications that use Mozilla’s trust store or versions derived from it and do not receive OneCRL updates.

Mozilla believes everyone has a fundamental right to security and privacy online. We remain committed to defending those rights and acting quickly to protect users.

Transparency is essential to trust. We will share more information as soon as circumstances allow.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: PHP warns it plans to release 2 emergency patches imminently
items.content:
Website admins, brace yourselves. Fixes for what are believed to be uncommonly severe vulnerabilities are scheduled to drop in a little more than 12 hours for PHP, a programming language that powers websites and Web applications everywhere.

PHP maintainers said Monday that they planned to release patches for two vulnerabilities, both with severity ratings of 9.2 out of a possible 10.

“All PHP users are encouraged to prepare now so they can upgrade as soon as the release is available,” the advisory stated. “We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild.”

The maintainers published the advisory following the leaking of purported details, which have yet to be confirmed. The report showed a video of an exploit tool dubbed PHP2Shell executing code on webservers running WordPress 7.1.3, MediaWiki 1.46.2, phpBB 3.3.17, Magento 2.4.9, Joomla 6.2.0, Laravel 13.36.0, Laravel 8.83.29, Symphony 8.1.9, Drupal 11.4.10, and WHMCS 9.0.9, all of which use PHP. A video depicting the tool has been reposted here .

Attempts to locate the unconfirmed report were unsuccessful, but security firm watchTowr said it claimed to affect every PHP version from PHP 5, released in 2004, onward. The security firm went on to say it has confirmed that the vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are real.

Researchers from separate security firm Sansec said they “expect mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release.” A third security firm, Webfence, also urged admins to prepare now. Huntress has also issued an advisory.

Preparation steps include identifying who is responsible for managing PHP inside an organization, taking an inventory of every app built on the language, planning a maintenance window starting at 14:00 UTC with contingency plans for earlier, making a backup of site and database files, and monitoring the PHP.net homepage for any late-breaking announcements, including an earlier release time. Some experts suggest unplugging any non-essential systems until they’re patched.

As an open source scripting language for building dynamic websites and web apps, PHP has come to be a de facto building block for the Web. It runs multiple CMS apps in addition to WordPress and also powers many internal tools. One security researcher said an estimated 1.3 million Internet-connected hosts are likely affected. Vulnerabilities with the severity the advisories are describing have the potential to inflict major damage across the Internet. Admins should remain aware that the patches can be released at any moment and remain vigilant until they do.

items.title: How I got over 300 Tor exit nodes removed
items.content:
On Friday Oct 2, 09:35am, 333 infected exit nodes started a coordinated campaign to intercept SSH connections and gather as much unencrypted data as possible.

To give you a sense of scale, all of Tor has around 3000 exit relays, so roughly 10% were under their control.

The attackers had gained access to the servers two months earlier, in August, and quietly deployed their Ebury 1.8.3 payload (an OpenSSH backdoor and credential stealer for Linux).

The attack appears to have had two primary goals:

By blocking certain ports, they made their exit nodes handle only unencrypted mail traffic.

An interesting writeup by one of the victims (a veteran Tor operator) goes into great detail about that:

In this post I'll focus on the second attack, the SSH MITM.

If you happen to get a circuit that exits over one of those 333 infected exit nodes, you won't notice anything at first.

Encrypted web traffic is forwarded as usual, but if you attempt an SSH connection over Port 22, you're unknowingly redirected to one of 12 SSH interception servers.

That's exactly what happened to me on Friday morning.

My SSH connection got redirected, and I was greeted with this warning:

But if you ignore the warning and go ahead with the login, the attacker does three things:

On Friday evening I contacted the Tor Project's network health team with my findings.

They confirmed this was something new and got to work by contacting the affected relay operators.

In their announcement, the health team described the pattern:

You can see the impact of those 333 exit nodes being shut down.

On metrics.torproject.org a clear dip is visible on October 4th and has not recovered since.

Consider running a relay: community.torproject.org/relay/setup/

In this part I'll go into detail about how I found all the infected exit nodes.

Using exitmap , I built a simple script that did the following:

it pinned an exit node, then opened an SSH connection from my server A to my server B.

I ran the script against every single one of the ~3000 exit relays.

Around a dozen served a fake fingerprint, and over 300 didn't intercept anything but redirected through those same interception servers.

Redirecting alone was enough to confirm the exit was infected.

In some further analysis I used sshesame as a honeypot.

Tricking the MITM into logging into the honeypot showed that they used paramiko (a Python SSH library) and also how they attempted to install Ebury using Perl.

Checking for permissions first, then executing a base64-encoded command.

The biggest question is still how they got into all those servers in the first place.

One theory is that the hosting company itself was hacked

(discussed here: lists.torproject.org ).

But that's just a theory floating around. In truth, no one really knows.

The use of Ebury and the broad collection of unencrypted data point to a financially motivated crime group.

I also suspect they deliberately launched their attack on a Friday, hoping that no one would want to ruin their weekend by responding.

All the more credit to the Tor Team for acting so quickly!

items.content:
Setting up SSH keys on macOS with Touch ID

In the first part of this post I’ll show a simple, secure way to create an SSH key on Mac (it’s 3 commands, including support for GitHub). In the second part I’ll dig deeper and explain what’s actually happening for the curious reader.

Macs have a built-in so-called Secure Enclave , where we can create “identities” that simply cannot be stolen (unless maybe you’ve made enemies with a nation state). Those identities are protected with Touch ID and can be used for SSH authentication. There are some great benefits about using this over traditional SSH key files:

The private material cannot be extracted, is never shown, cannot be stolen,

You get prompted whenever the identity is used,

No key files (like ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub and friends) littering the file system; and there’s no risk of mistakenly deleting them either.

This extra security will be in effect whenever you use SSH, including git-over-ssh like GitHub. It’s great that advanced security tech is available by default on some of the most widely distributed computers in the world! A few years ago stuff like this could only be found at CERN and/or in Dan Brown novels. Let’s see how it can be set up on your consumer-grade Mac.

It is essential that the human interface be designed for ease of use, so that users routinely and automatically apply the protection mechanisms correctly.

Saltzer and Schroeder, “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems”

We’ll create a secure identity on the Secure Enclave, then tell SSH how to use it for authentication, and finally add the key to GitHub.

Step 1: create the identity that you’ll use on this Mac:

sc_auth create-ctk-identity -l ssh-key -k p-256-ne -t bio # run once to create identity

You’ll be prompted to touch “Touch ID”. Your identity is now created and saved securely (parameters are explained in the deep dive below).

Step 2: tell SSH to use the identity (when prompted for a PIN, just hit enter):

ssh-add -K -S /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib # run after a reboot

From here on, SSH will know to use the identity from the Secure Enclave when connecting via SSH; it does not have a good memory so you’ll need to remind it after a reboot.

Step 3: Whenever you need to register your key to a new server (like GitHub), run this command:

ssh-add -L # run when you need the public key

If multiple identities are listed, use the line that starts with sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256... . It’s a shareable handle for the identity, and this is the SSH key that GitHub will ask about.

The output of ssh-add -L can be added as a GitHub SSH Key

That’s all you need for a super secure setup! The new identity can now be used with SSH, and you’ll be prompted for Touch ID during authentication:

No one can steal your identity (well, you can’t even give it away willingly since it can’t be extracted from the Secure Enclave), but with great powers etc: if your Mac dies, so does the identity, and you’ll need to create a new one (and re-register it where necessary, like GitHub).

You’ll get a Touch ID prompt when git tries to authenticate with SSH

If you’re curious about how this works, read on!

We’ll now try to understand what happens under the hood. We’ll start with the actual identity creation in the Secure Enclave, then look at how SSH is allowed to interface with the Secure Enclave with ssh-keychain.dylib , and then try to see what happens in a complete SSH sign-in flow.

This is the result of reading posts (like this great investigation by arianvp ), manual pages, and experimentation. A lot of this is undocumented, and this is the minimum information I needed to form a mental model of what’s happening and convince myself that it does, indeed, work.

Some of the command outputs below have been trimmed for legibility, I invite you to run them locally if you want the full experience!

Creating an identity on the Secure Enclave

items.title: NixOS is making me less afraid
items.content:
On the go? Listen to an ai -narrated version of this article .

Something funny happened a little while ago: I read about FreshRSS, and it

sounded nice, so I installed it on a server and started using it . That would

not have happened a year ago, but then again, a year ago I didn’t have any NixOS

For the past few years, my rss feeds have lived locally on my phone only.

There was a good idea behind that 1 1 I can mostly take time to read when I’m

away from my computer anyway. , but it never quite worked in practice. For one,

many things are easier to read on a larger screen. But it was also brittle to

trust a phone app to manage the read/unread status of thousands of articles

across a hundred feeds. 2 2 In particular, when I switched to a different phone

I could migrate all feeds to it, but the read/unread status was lost along the

way. What I really wanted was a server-side feed aggregator. This is software

that runs on a server, manages rss feeds, and then I can read the rss feeds

either through a web interface, or through client applications. I’ve wanted that

for a while, but I’ve never taken the step, because it would be yet another side

But now, with some NixOS experience, adding a working FreshRSS configuration

(including backups) took 9 lines of Nix code 3 3 Plus a dozen more lines for the

nginx reverse proxy configuration. It got a little complicated because I wanted

to proxy_pass from a specific location block which required rewriting cookie

paths. But that’s a me problem, not a NixOS problem. . That installation has

just hands-off worked for the past few months. If or when that server breaks, I

can spin up a new one running the exact same configuration, probably in

something like 15 minutes. When we can do something like that, there is

literally no reason to not just try the new software.

Contrast this against how FreshRSS is installed outside of NixOS. Then we’d

download and extract an archive to the right location;

configure permissions according to instructions;

install nginx and php-fpm with necessary extra dependencies to the server;

configure php-fpm pools and make nginx pass requests through to php-fpm ;

hopefully remember how to do all the above if something breaks and we need to

reinstall FreshRSS on a new or upgraded server later.

Of course, the FreshRSS project provides a container image which would shorten

the process a little bit. It purports to set up Apache with mod_php and

configure them the right way. Then we’d only need to configure backups, create a

systemd service that runs the container, and manage nginx as a tls terminating

reverse proxy in front of that, because the container image reasonably does not

come with tls support. This is still stuff to remember, and there’s also no

guarantee the same thing works six months down the line when reinstalling,

unless we wrote down which exact container image we downloaded. 4 4 It does not

help to build the container image from source, because two builds from the same

Dockerfile separated by time can result in rather different container images.

I have mentioned before how much I dislike maintaining side projects. That

includes my own code, but also self-hosted services developed by someone else.

I’m okay with a few minutes of maintenance here and there, but having to

schedule hours of uninterrupted work to upgrade something, or spending any

amount of time at all on emergency maintenance, really kills my desire to work

You’d think someone of my disposition would be deep into configuration

management, container orchestration, or both, but no. I have made honest

attempts with CFEngine, Ansible, podman, and k3s but none of them improved my

installation/configuration/deployment experience significantly over (a)

carefully writing things down, and sometimes (b) turning those careful notes

into a shell script performing a sequence of ssh commands. 5 5 Yes, this is

essentially reinventing Ansible – but less…

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Elon Musk confirms talks to merge Tesla and SpaceX
items.content:
Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX

2 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google

Elon Musk is chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla

Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies.

"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts to discuss SpaceX's latest results on Tuesday.

While Musk noted it could not be assumed a merger will go ahead, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies had been formed to examine the move.

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," he said. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."

With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.

SpaceX builds space rockets as well as Starlink internet satellites and provides a secured satellite network for governments, including the US, through its Starshield business.

That part of the business is currently facing scrutiny over claims Ukraine's access to the network has been limited, leaving it vulnerable to deadly strikes by Russia.

US President Donald Trump has denied either he or Musk ordered the slowdown . Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions.

Starlink's total revenue rose to $5.2bn in the three months to 30 September from $3bn in the same period last year. It is dwarfed by SpaceX's expansion into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, such as Anthropic and Google.

The business generated revenues of $7.5bn over the three months, up from $813m last year.

Why does Elon Musk want to merge Tesla and SpaceX?

Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger.

He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of both Tesla and SpaceX.

Even commenting on the possibility of combining the two companies, Musk compared it to "tap dancing through a minefield".

A merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, he added. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve a combination, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".

Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued at around $1tn.

While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics.

SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its market debut in June.

Elon Musk and Donald Trump have denied limiting Ukraine's access to SpaceX's Starshield network

SpaceX, as a whole is not profitable, despite revenue jumping to $27bn from $13.7bn over the first nine months of the year.

Over that same period it lost $1.1bn although it did report a $4.4bn profit for the most recent three months.

Following Musk's comments, SpaceX's share price rose 8% in after-hours trading. Shares in Tesla, which reports its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose by 2%

Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X , the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned.

The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together.

items.title: The terrifying liminal space between code-writer and bot-prompter
items.content:
Disclaimer: These are my own thoughts and opinions. They don’t reflect those of my employer. I’m discussing my own personal feelings about AI. I think it’s fair to say everyone is having to grapple with this tech, whether it’s how to use it or how to avoid it. The following represents a snapshot of my grappling, nothing more.

LLM coding advancements both impress and terrify me and I don’t know what I think about it or how to cope with it. I feel like I will be able to build things I never have been able to before, but at the same time, I have heightened fears about being replaceable or less valuable in my job. If all I’m doing is prompting an AI bot, why am I being paid so much?

When I work with an LLM coding harness [1] it usually makes me feel uneasy. It feels like my name is going to be attached to something I didn’t really do. Sure, I could review the code. But it’s still not my code. Constantly reviewing LLM-generated code is mentally fatiguing and is not enjoyable in the way coding is. And at a certain point, it really becomes a challenge to keep up with code review. Before long, you find yourself skimming and saying, “That seems right.”

A developer who is skilled with and/or enjoys working with this stuff would probably say you don’t need to review the code. Trust the LLM, trust the tests. As much as I hate it, I think that might actually be right. Trying to keep up pace with a bot that can spew out thousands of lines of code in minutes seems like a fool’s errand.

The models are good now. That’s the refrain I’ve been hearing for the last six months. Again, as much as I hate to admit it, I have to agree the models are much better than they were. I’m routinely impressed, particularly in the GPT models. A year ago, hallucinations seemed to be more of a problem. Nowadays, the LLM will search the internet, search the code, and run its own experiments before taking a stab at answering your questions. I don’t know if it’s the models that are that much better, or if it’s a huge improvement of the harnesses. Probably both.

You’re probably sick of hearing this, but if you haven’t used one of these coding tools in the last six months, you probably don’t have a good idea of what they are capable of .

But I hate it. Why do I hate it? I just have this icky feeling when I use it. And that’s not even considering all the other big negatives like how it kinda feels like these companies stole from everyone. Or the negative environmental effects. Or all the mindless slop that’s everywhere now.

There’s obviously a lot of doom-mongering in the industry. The companies making this stuff say AI is going to take our jobs or, I shit you not, kill everyone . So that’s… good .

But let’s assume for a moment that the worst-case scenarios aren’t true. What does software development look like in the future? I’m worried about being replaced, but maybe I’ll be even more valuable. If the cost to produce software drops, Jevons paradox says people will consume even more software. If demand for software goes up, well, I’m someone who can produce software (or begrudgingly facilitate a machine producing it). I have soft skills and insights around my technical knowledge, and maybe that continues to be valuable.

So I just go back and forth. I worry about it, but then I think everything will work out. It’s something that’s been on my mind a lot this past year. I can’t just quit tech to become a gardener . As someone with spinal muscular atrophy, some kind of knowledge work is all I can do. The government programs that I use for my daily care don’t cover 100% of my needs. Without my income, I would be very near needing to live in a nursing home.

So I’m keeping watch. I’m staying open minded and trying to find a path forward in this new world.

Usually either Claude Code in the terminal or Codex via the ChatGPT app. ↩︎

The views expressed here are mine and no one else’s.

Voxtral 3 introduces a cutting-edge voice agent SDK and state-of-the-art speech models designed for real-time, multi-step conversations across 50+ languages. It combines accurate transcription, natural speech synthesis with emotional adaptability, and deep tool integration for seamless workflow automation. Available via Mistral’s EU-hosted API or self-deployment, it ensures data sovereignty while delivering low-latency, human-like interactions for contact centers, virtual assistants, and hands-free copilots.

Speech transcription and voice generation have come a long way, but building end-to-end voice agents that can listen, reason, interact, and handle complex workflows remains difficult.

A reliable voice agent needs to do four things very well (and simultaneously):

Listen accurately across languages, accents, speakers, and interruptions,

Reason deeply about what users mean in specific contexts,

Speak naturally with emotion and expression, and

Take action over multiple steps through connected systems.

Getting all four to work together reliably in real time remains a challenge.

To address this, we introduce Voxtral 3: a new family of state-of-the-art speech-to-text and text-to-speech models, alongside a voice agent SDK that brings listening, thinking, tool calling, and speaking into a single real-time streaming pipeline.

Voxtral 3 is built to create natural conversational experiences, from contact-center agents and service desks to virtual assistants and hands-free copilots. With support for dozens of languages, expressive speech, complex reasoning, and deep integration with your own tools and data, agents built with Voxtral can interpret nuanced intent, reason through sophisticated requests, and execute multi-step actions across connected systems.

As with other Mistral models, the Voxtral 3 family is designed for sovereign deployment. Available today through Mistral's EU-hosted API or for self-deployment on your own infrastructure, it gives organizations control over where audio is processed, how data is handled, and whether conversations are retained.

Accurate transcription across 50+ languages . The speech-to-text model, Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 , is state-of-the-art in multilingual transcription, identifying who said what (diarization), using keyphrases to improve its accuracy (context-biasing). It detects when someone has finished speaking so agents can respond without delay (end-of-turn detection).

Natural speech that adapts to the conversation . The text-to-speech model, Voxtral Mini TTS 3 , introduces new voices that adjust their emotion, pace, and emphasis based on conversational context, with support for 35+ languages and 50+ dialects.

Human-like intelligence at your (spoken) command . The new voice agent SDK combines listening, reasoning, tool calling, and speaking into a real-time experience. Agents can retrieve information, interact with business systems, and complete tasks during live conversations over phone or web.

Pro Voice for distinctly accurate voice adaptation . For professional use cases where basic voice cloning does not suffice, Voxtral’s Pro Voice adaptation is able to reproduce a speaker’s distinctive character, emotional range, and speaking style across languages, using just 30 minutes of audio.

items.title: The Future of CSS
items.content:
For the past few years, all of the major browser vendors (Google, Apple, Microsoft, and Mozilla, along with Igalia and Bocoup) have been working together on Interop (opens in new tab) , a project to improve universal browser support on web technologies. It’s been a remarkably successful effort; when a focus area gets added to Interop, it often winds up reaching near-100% support across all major browsers within a year. ✨ CSS Subgrid is a good example. Subgrid is a super-powerful extension to CSS Grid which enables entirely new layouts . It was implemented in Firefox back in 2019, but there wasn’t much movement with other browsers for years. It got added to Interop 2023, and by the end of that year, it was widely available across all modern browsers: The Y axis shows the percentage of tests related to subgrid passing in each browser. The black “Interop” line shows tests passing in all browsers. As we reach the end of 2026, Interop 2027 is currently being planned, and the team at Mozilla has created a ranking system (opens in new tab) for us to upvote our most-requested features. They plan on using the ranking data to decide what to include for next year’s Interop! In this blog post, I want to dig into the top 10 features I voted for, to offer a bit of a preview of what CSS might look like within the next year. There will also be some little tips and tricks you can start using today! Current as of October 2026 . items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Apple broke an essential presentation feature of iPads
items.content:
A brief digression from my usual teaching posts to complain about a devastating regression in iPadOS 27.

If you’ve followed my work up until now, you’ll know that I rely heavily on writing on handouts from my iPad, projected via AirPlay to an external screen that my students can see. When I’m doing this, my iPad is also doing many other things: controlling a PowerPoint presentation on my Mac , showing me notes that I’ve taken on points I want to mention and students I want to call on, and showing me the results of polls before I reveal them to the class. This ability to do other things on your iPad while the audience just sees your presentation or handout is an essential part of a variety of pedagogical moves that I use in my teaching.

Unfortunately, Apple just completely broke it.

As of iPadOS 27, if you have multiple windows open while AirPlaying (whether or not Stage Manager is on), tapping on anything other than the presenting app will snap the external display into showing your whole iPad screen. This means that my students see all my notes on who I want to call on, or poll results that should be hidden from them. They also get distracted from what we’re learning by all these jarring windows popping up and disappearing. If you’re presenting at a big conference, it’s extremely embarrassing.

In GoodNotes, the presenter view will return once you tap back on the app. In Keynote, it will just exit the presentation entirely. In PowerPoint, it will put the app in a limbo where you have to restart the presentation to proceed. Here’s a Reddit post illustrating the behavior in GoodNotes . But don’t just take my word for it; try it at home!

I sort of understand why Apple did this. In iPadOS 26, which app could “control” the external display was hard to identify. Essentially, you had to swipe up as though going to the home screen, then tap on the app you wanted in the dock, and that app would take over the external display if it had a presentation mode. This was weird and hard to understand, but Apple’s solution is to just make it so that whatever is the most recently tapped app takes over, which is much, much worse.

As for what the behavior should be, I’m not a developer, but here’s a proposal: if you’re using an app that is in presenter mode (e.g., PowerPoint playing a presentation, or a GoodNotes document open), it should always get precedence on the external display, until that presentation gets stopped, the document is closed, or the app is quit. Period.

I talked/griped/whined/begged about this on an episode of Mac Power Users in early September ( here’s a link to the video ), and as of now this behavior hasn’t changed, including in the latest betas. I’m hoping that this post can get the word out, or that maybe someone has figured out a workaround. I’ve also filed a feedback report with Apple and encourage you to do the same ( click here and mention my feedback code FB23615646).

I’ll update this post if anything changes, but for now, I can’t recommend this operating system to anyone using their iPad to teach or present.

items.title: Mastodon 5.0: A closer look
items.content:
October is here, and it’s almost time for Mastodon’s 5.0 release! We announced our plans for big changes in an early preview back in August. In this companion article, we’re hoping to shed light on some of the decisions behind this major UI overhaul.

Between the feedback we’ve gathered during Discovery Week, an event in which we spent a week doing surveys and workshop sessions with volunteers from the community, and Mastodon’s 10th anniversary coming up, we were determined to deliver something notable.

Working on Mastodon’s engineering team can sometimes feel like harvesting wheat one stalk at a time. We make a lot happen with limited resources–far more limited than most people realise–but there’s always more to do. There’s more tech and UX debt than is obvious to the naked eye, so something that seems simple on the outside may be often limited by backend constraints or architecture shifts that can’t easily be changed. So we had to make concessions about what we could realistically fit into our 5.0 plans, and leave some work for later.

What’s better for one person can be worse for another, and we’ve had to keep that in mind throughout the redesign. We’re acutely aware that such a divide is most pronounced between longstanding users and newcomers. Mastodon’s current UI is beloved by many longtime users, since it can be very powerful once you’ve learned its secrets and quirks. However, newcomers should be able to dive in without being overwhelmed. To keep the community fresh, alive and diverse, we need to break down the barriers to joining, so when you bring your friends, they can find their way around without a manual.

The redesign was grounded in these principles:

Clarity trumps convenience. The most powerful interface can be useless if it’s too difficult to figure out. Making things more clear and obvious can result in more friction, and that can be necessary.

Leave room for what’s to come. Navigation may feel emptier for now, and that is on purpose. We have lots of improvements planned that we need to leave space for, to avoid moving more elements around in the future.

Small improvements matter. We might not be able to fix everything overnight, but we’ll continue to look for small but meaningful improvements to accessibility and usability.

Our previous blog post covers most of the big stuff: We’re moving away from the embedded composer and adopting a pop-out composer with new controls for visibility and other post settings. Navigation is simplified and organised in a more intuitive way and create space for future new features.

The desktop 5.0 web interface showing the post composer opened at the bottom of the main column.

In your feeds, the posts themselves have been rebuilt from the ground up, giving a fresh look to the places we all spend the most time. We’re also excited to roll out a few new colour themes, which took a truly monumental effort from our engineering team since the start of the year to tokenise our design system.

The web interface, changing between the five available theme colours.

The new design includes many small affordances, such as hiding a user’s boosts directly from the post menu, following and unfollowing hashtags right from the post, and hiding your own posts and boosts in your home feed.

Under Advanced Settings, two new options allow you to decide if your own boosts and posts appear in your main feed.

Notable iterations (since the August blog post)

Since our original announcement, we’ve iterated a lot on the feedback we’ve been receiving, so you’ll notice that the UI looks a bit different than what we’ve shown in that blog post. Here’s what’s changed:

From bottom right to bottom centre : The position of the composer in the bottom right was controversial. The biggest complaint was that the composer was so far away from the main navigation. items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Battle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensifies days before Brazil presidential runoff
items.content:
Brazilians protested outside Meta’s headquarters in São Paulo this week, alleging the tech firm restricted Lula’s reach. Photograph: Nelson Almeida/AFP/Getty Images

Brazilians protested outside Meta’s headquarters in São Paulo this week, alleging the tech firm restricted Lula’s reach. Photograph: Nelson Almeida/AFP/Getty Images

Battle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensifies days before Brazil presidential runoff

Lula’s supporters suspect tech firm meddling on behalf of US president Donald Trump, who has close ties to Bolsonaro family

F ive days after his defeat in the first round of the Brazilian presidential election, leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spent almost 24 hours unable to boost his Instagram posts, while his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, could.

Lula’s lawyers included the episode in a list of incidents that they submitted to the electoral court and international observers as “evidence” that Meta, Instagram’s owner, was actively trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour.

Reports from Lula supporters saying their content had been removed or its reach restricted flooded social media in Brazil, while about a dozen watchdogs and research groups published reports describing what they called “indications” that Meta may have favoured the senator’s campaign.

Meta called Lula’s allegations “false and unfounded”, saying there had been “technical incidents” that affected campaigns from “different parts of the political spectrum”.

The controversy fuelled the electoral battle between Lula and Bolsonaro just days before next Sunday’s runoff and gained further traction after the electoral court ordered Meta not to give the candidates “unequal treatment”.

Brazil cuts work week to 40 hours in win for Lula ahead of runoff

Late last week, justice Marco Aurélio Bellizze said he had found no evidence of deliberate action by the company, which would require further investigation, but he gave Meta 24 hours to prove that the problems affecting Lula had been fixed and would not happen again.

On Monday, after saying the company had failed to do so, Bellizze gave Meta a further 24 hours . The company responded on Tuesday, again denying any favouritism and saying it had introduced human review to prevent any automated restrictions.

Meta has denied any favouritism in the contest between Lula, right, and Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro. Photograph: Allison Sales/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Meta’s oversight board, a quasi-independent body whose decisions are binding, issued a statement saying it was “concerned by recurring enforcement failures in Meta’s election integrity efforts”, citing both Brazil’s election and the suspension of the anti-Trump No Kings movement’s account in the US for several hours last Saturday, during demonstrations aimed at encouraging early voting in the midterm elections.

items.content:
A new version of C# is coming soon, so we're continuing our annual tradition of reviewing its new features. The Microsoft team has prepared several highly anticipated and exciting changes for this release. Let's take a look at them.

We'll start with the most straightforward change, union types. They enable developers to combine types without relying on inheritance or interfaces where it's unnecessary or unavailable. A union is a structure that contains the complete set of supported types.

In the code above, union is the keyword, while int , Version , and IEnumerable<string> are the set of supported types.

The union types come in handy when traditional inheritance isn't an option, as it requires the types to have something in common. However, there may be cases where inheritance is impossible or makes little architectural sense. We might need to handle a specific set of types, including primitives. Normally, we'd have to specify a variable of the object type as input and then cast it to the required types within the method, including logic for handling anything unsupported. That's error-prone. Using union in this situation would solve these problems, making the code safer and easier to read.

Given the nature of the new structure, when we use union , the compiler already knows the complete list of types it can contain. So, the default branch is no longer necessary. The change protects us from a switch that misses some types while new subclasses keep falling into the default section, which can cause unpredictable program behavior.

Let's look at a more specific example. Before this update, we'd have had to write something like this to define a method for handling API responses:

The ApiResult abstract class, from which specific responses inherit, is declared. So, if a new subclass appears and the developer fails to handle it, executions falls into the default branch. With a union , it works differently:

As you can see, there's no need for a parent class just to group the types together. The behavior is also more predictable because the compiler knows at compile time exactly which types union can contain. So, if a switch doesn't handle every type in the union, the compiler issues a warning.

Moreover, the union gives developers an easier way to express patterns such as monads. It also enables implementing custom methods and properties within union , so working with all its types doesn't require writing switch .

This change is somewhat related to union in that it also lets the compiler know exactly how many types it'll work with. It does so by preventing inheritance from a class outside the assembly where it was declared. This behavior resembles a mix of internal and sealed : it takes the scope from internal and the restriction on inheritance from sealed . This can be useful, for example, in libraries where we want to restrict inheritance from certain classes without blocking it within our own assembly. Here's an example declaration:

The closed keyword marks the class as closed to inheritance. As a result, attempting to inherit from such a class in another assembly causes a compilation error. Note that, like union , a closed hierarchy supports an exhaustive switch , which enables omitting the default branch.

items.title: What shall I teach my son?
items.content:
What is the purpose of education in the age of AGI?

Yesterday, the title The End of Education by Neil Postman called to me from my bookshelf, whispering that it might be the right book at the right time. It was. Published in 1995, it was surprisingly appropriate balm for the soul of a confused programmer and soon-to-be father.

My wife and I are expecting our first child. My economically valuable skillset – programming – suddenly feels less valuable. What shall I teach my son? And to what end?

That the radio will supplant the teacher.

Already one may learn languages by means

Teachers will be relegated to the backwoods.

Perhaps I can get a position at the switchboard.

– Quoted in The End of Education by Neil Postman, quoting Teachers and Machines: The Use of Technology Since 1920 by Larry Cuban

Books will soon be obsolete in the public schools… Our school system will be completely changed inside of ten years.

– Thomas Edison, The New York Dramatic Mirror, 1913

Back in 2013 , I boldly predicted that MOOCs would upend education. Ah, my past self, you sweet summer child.

Nassim Nicholas Taleb has helped me appreciate the staying power of staying power, sometimes called The Lindy Effect . Merely staying alive implies some anti-fragility to adapt and survive. Consider that Harvard, Yale, and Princeton were founded to educate the clergy. From The End of Education:

In the Western world, beginning in the thirteenth century and for five hundred years afterward, that God was sufficient justification for the founding of institutions of learning, from grammar schools, where children were taught to read the Bible, to great universities, where men were trained to be ministers of God.

Schools survived what happened to religion. It should be no surprise that they’ve survived the radio, motion pictures, and the internet.

We typically confuse why something claims it exists, ie to glorify God, vs the forces that actually perpetuate it, which are subtler, we’d prefer not spoken aloud, and more prosaic, ie endowments, prestige, and needing someone to watch one’s kids.

It has been a surprisingly good bet that schools will continue to exist in roughly their current form for many years to come. Ironically, there also seems to be some staying power to technologists boldly (and so far incorrectly) doubting the staying power of schools! I myself have contributed to this grand tradition multiple times, and find myself at risk of doing it yet again.

Surely this time must finally be different, right? We have captured intelligence in a bottle, and you’re telling me that “Ok class, turn to page 17” and “Does anyone know how to solve for x” are still going to be around in the 2030s?

There are many shifting purposes to education, which underpin how it has survived this long. As the times change, so do its purposes shift and adapt, such as:

I once tried to come up with a single-word purpose for education, and I landed upon the word “resourceful”, because I reasoned that if you “were able to use arbitrary resources to uncover and solve problems”, you had no more need for schooling. In the age of Google, email, and the internet, a person was educated when they could wield them. But now I see my vision of resourcefulness perfected in the AI agent and its tool loop. Maybe resourcefulness will go the way of the Dewey Decimal System which in turn supplanted memorization and an oral tradition.

Imagine education as a table held up by its many purposes. I didn’t realize how centrally important “the ability to earn a living” was for me until it started to wobble. A big reason is because I’m looking for a more objective arbiter of “good” in education. Education’s own tests and measures can feel stifling. The market offered a counterpoint. Steve Jobs and Bill Gates were college dropouts, but the market deemed them good. Now that I think of it, apparently Einstein was a mediocre student, but his contributions to science were his way out. With recent…

items.title: Updates to site guidelines and AI/LLM tags
items.content:
I've been having to perform an increasing number of moderation actions surrounding the vibecoding tag and AI/LLM related content. I started reading Lobsters because it had the most interesting viewpoints related to computing. During that time, I've found that this community is at it's best when it's trying to, in good faith, help others grow. In lieu of a larger and more rambling discussion on this point, we would like to try two changes encourage that behavior again and re-focus topicality around ensuring that content submitted to the site should, at a minimum, be respectful of a reader's time and intelligence.

The first adjustment is two updates to the about page, which try to provide a bit more clarity in what we consider topical and what constitutes self promotion:

Lobsters is a computing-focused community centered around discussing links. Our goal is to learn, craft, collaborate, and share interesting viewpoints.

The administrator is Peter Bhat Harkins ("pushcx"), contact him or another moderator with any support issues. Lobsters was launched on July 3rd, 2012 by joshua stein  (who is no longer running it, so please quit bugging him with site stuff) with careful design touches to encourage a healthy community:

At this risk of writing a mission statement, it seemed worth explaining what the site is and hopes to be to visitors from the first sentence of /about. (This original text came from an intro post .)

Topicality: Lobsters is focused pretty narrowly on computing; tags like art don't imply every piece of art is on-topic.  Some rules of thumb for great stories to submit: Will this improve the reader's next program? Will it deepen their understanding of their last program? Will it be more interesting in five or ten years? Is this compelling material that will seed a discussion, or is it just an artifact?

Pending an upcoming deploy, we no longer allow submissions which are code repositories. While, at first blush, this may seem odd for a community which is primarily centered around programming but it does eliminate the bulk of the "low effort, self promotional" submissions we've been seeing on the site. We've also found that being dropped into a new codebase doesn't start discussions because the reader has to have enough subject matter experience to immediately recognize what's novel or otherwise worth talking about. Instead, we are more interested in content around code bases which cover why it was created, the purpose it serves, the challenges overcome, and the reasons why it's a useful artifact in the ecosystem.

Some things that are off-topic here but popular on larger, similar sites: entrepreneurship; management; careers; news about companies that employ a lot of programmers; investing; world events; anthropology; self-help; personal productivity systems; last-resort customer service requests via public shaming; "I wanted to see what this site's amazing users think about this off-topic thing"; and defining the single morally correct economic and political system for the entire world when we can't even settle tabs vs. spaces.

We're listing "careers" as off-topic to try to head off posts about interviewing, promotions, burnout, and farming . We have the  job tag because it's nice to help people connect to jobs, but the topic of getting a good job, weaving jobs into a career over your lifetime, and work is a different thing than the actual programming itself.

Self-promotion: It's great to have authors participate in the community, but we do not want the community to be exploited as a write-only tool for product announcements or driving traffic to their work. As a rule of thumb, self-promotional activity should be less than a quarter of one's stories and comments in the last year. New users ( first 70 days ) are not allowed to submit self-promo.

items.title: PHP warns admins of two critical flaws, emergency patches coming tomorrow: plans to release security updates on Wednesday, October 21, at 14:00 UTC (10:00 AM Eastern).
items.content:
PHP warns admins of two critical flaws, emergency patches coming tomorrow

The PHP security team is warning administrators to prepare for emergency security updates tomorrow to address two critical vulnerabilities, as information about the flaws has reportedly leaked ahead of their scheduled disclosure.

PHP powers many websites and web applications, including content management systems, e-commerce platforms, and custom web services.

In an advisory published Tuesday , the PHP development team announced that it plans to release security updates on Wednesday, October 21, at 14:00 UTC (10:00 AM Eastern), to address two vulnerabilities, each rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0.

The PHP security team also sent a notice to its ANNOUNCE mailing list, urging administrators to prepare to install the security updates as soon as they become available.

"We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild," the PHP security team warned.

The developers have not disclosed any technical details about the vulnerabilities, including which PHP versions are affected, how they can be exploited, or which releases will contain fixes.

However, security researchers at watchTowr told BleepingComputer that the vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are remote code execution (RCE) flaws believed to affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8.

"In the last hour, two remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP have been leaked. These vulnerabilities were previously scheduled under embargo and due for release on Thursday at 11 am ET," watchTowr CEO Benjamin Harris told BleepingComputer.

"While we are not able to share technical information at this point for obvious reasons, given the sensitivity, we can confirm that these vulnerabilities are indeed real. Both of them are CVSS10 and are understood to affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8."

watchTowr also said it believes it has successfully reproduced CVE-2026-109618 but is not releasing technical information until security patches become available.

The researchers clarified that they have not observed exploitation of the vulnerabilities in the wild, despite the information reportedly leaking ahead of the planned disclosure.

In a post on X , watchTowr warned that information about the vulnerabilities had leaked before the originally planned disclosure date.

"We were all supposed to wait until Thursday at 11am ET. Information has leaked wrt zero-day embargoed RCE vulns in PHP. We can confirm that they're real," the researchers said.

The warning follows a now-deleted post on Y Combinator's Hacker News forum, in which a user named "petecooper" claimed that two critical PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities would be disclosed on October 22.

The post, seen by BleepingComputer, claimed that both vulnerabilities carried CVSS scores of 10.0 and affected PHP versions dating back to PHP 5.

It also identified the vulnerabilities as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, matching the identifiers watchTowr later shared.

However, watchTowr's statements and the Hacker News post are different from PHP's official announcement. Both described the vulnerabilities as CVSS 10.0, while the PHP security team assigned each a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2.

Additionally, watchTowr cited an originally planned Thursday disclosure, while PHP has officially scheduled its security release for tomorrow morning.

The PHP security team says it will publish full technical details, affected versions, and fixed releases when the security updates become available.
