items.title: Ofcom concedes defeat in 4chan case
items.content:
Insofar as a political organization like Ofcom is even capable of admitting defeat, it did so in the 4chan enforcement today.

In testimony before the Commons Digital, Culture, Media, and Sport Committee, Ofcom admitted it knows its jurisdiction ends where a foreign court’s jurisdiction begins.

“We won’t be able to recover every single fine on online safety. If foreign courts decide to try and get in our way, there will be a point at which we have to accept that we won’t be able to recover that money.”

– Dame Melanie Dawes, Chief Executive, Ofcom

Guido Fawkes characterizes this admission thus: “ Ofcom Admits Defeat .”

Guido is right. American courts have, by now, provided their preliminary view on the likelihood of Ofcom’s enforcement powers being successful in U.S. courts – the obiter dicta in 4chan v. Ofcom , the opinion in the case we filed against Ofcom in the federal District Court for the District of Columbia a little over a year ago.

Those dicta made it awfully clear that Ofcom can expect a very chilly reception in an American courtroom if it ever tries to enforce its fines in the United States. By way of reminder, the Court in 4chan said:

Because Plaintiffs represent that they have “no presence, infrastructure, or operations abroad,” Pls.’ Opp’n at 5; Compl. paras. 20, 24, that likely means enforcing any judgment in the United States. At that point, Plaintiffs could avail themselves of the protection of American courts.

Unless Ofcom is prepared to sail a British invasion fleet here and land ground troops, enforcement would indeed have to proceed through American courts. Which presents the following problem for Ofcom:

American courts generally decline to enforce foreign judgments that violate the United States Constitution , if indeed Plaintiffs are correct in their constitutional claims. See, e.g. , Matusevitch v. Telnikoff , 877 F. Supp. 1, 4 (D.D.C. 1995) (refusing to enforce a British judgment because it contravened the First Amendment and was therefore “repugnant to the public policies of the State of Maryland and the United States”)[.]

Suffice it to say, 4chan’s constitutional arguments are correct.

The Court then added, gratuitously and sua sponte as this was not an issue which was actually briefed by either party in the case,

Finally, at the risk of gilding the lily, to the extent any foreign judgment against Plaintiffs were penal in nature, Plaintiffs may find a receptive audience before American courts regardless of the judgment’s compatibility with the United States Constitution. That is because American courts are not necessarily required to enforce foreign penal judgments[.]

Put another way, even though the Court ruled against 4chan on the sovereign immunity motion, the Court nonetheless went out of its way to communicate a message to Ofcom in this decision.

That message was: your writ doesn’t run here.

Losing the sovereign immunity motion was a price well worth paying for those dicta on enforceability and their associated deterrent value, especially considering that the only remedy 4chan sought from the D.D.C. – the one the Court couldn’t give due to sovereign immunity – was a declaration of the rights of the parties. What we got instead was the Court’s opinion as to the state of the law, inviting the parties to read between the lines; the substance of what 4chan had asked for, albeit in a different form.

Thus ended this dispute, for all practical purposes. Ofcom can’t enforce the Online Safety Act in America. Ofcom knows it, Ofcom has known it for a long time, and now, Ofcom has, finally, admitted it.

It would be a gift – to 4chan – if Ofcom decided to show up in an American court after all this, waiving sovereign immunity and thus facing the prospect of an adverse merits ruling in the process. Filing that lawsuit would be suicidal, leading to virtually certain defeat and total loss of enforcement credibility in the United States. It will almost certainly never happen, not for 4chan, and…

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Hands on With The Retroid Pocket Duo; A Little More Magic This Time
items.content:
A Familiar Design, a Different Kind of Duo

When I finished reviewing the Retroid Pocket Duo Lite, I found myself in a slightly unusual position. There were plenty of things about it that I could criticize, and its modest hardware certainly made some of the things I wanted to do more difficult than they needed to be, but I still really liked the little thing. Retroid has always had a knack for making handhelds that feel like toys in the very best sense of the word, and the Duo Lite was no exception. It was colorful, comfortable, wonderfully nostalgic, and I enjoyed picking it up and opening those two screens. SeedlessDS eventually became something of a saving grace for me, not because the other emulators were necessarily lacking, but because I enjoyed using it so much that it gave me another reason to keep coming back to the device. Still, I couldn't help wondering what this same design might be capable of with considerably more powerful hardware behind it.

Hands-On with Retroid Pocket Duo Lite; Not Quite Magic, But Close

Retroid gets the feel of two-screen gaming right, even if the hardware occasionally reminds you where the compromises were made.

My review of the Retroid Pocket Duo Lite

Well, that's where the Retroid Pocket Duo comes in. This is the most expensive member of Retroid's new dual-screen family, and while it shares much of its design with the cheaper Duo Lite, what's underneath those familiar plastics is quite different. For $269, you're getting Qualcomm's Dragonwing Q-7790 processor, 8GB of RAM, Android 16 and, perhaps most importantly, two rather lovely AMOLED displays running at 120Hz. The upper screen is a 5.5-inch 1920 × 1080 panel with a 16:9 aspect ratio, while the lower is a 4.5-inch 1280 × 960 display in the more traditional 4:3 format. It's an interesting combination, giving you a widescreen display for everything from PSP to modern Android games, while retaining a lower screen that feels much closer to the Nintendo handhelds that inspired this whole resurgence. There's also a revised shoulder and trigger arrangement, including proper analogue triggers, making this feel like a more ambitious device than simply a Duo Lite with better screens.

I've spent a fair amount of time with modern dual-screen handhelds over the last year or so, having reviewed the original Anbernic RG DS and its Plus successor, the AYN Thor Pro and Lite, and more recently Retroid's own Duo Lite. One thing that has become increasingly apparent to me is that there isn't really one ‘correct’ way to approach this form factor. Some of these machines are happiest when they're pretending to be a Nintendo DS, others have enough power to make the 3DS library feel right at home, while the more ambitious Android devices are beginning to explore things that Nintendo never attempted or dreamed of with its original hardware. The standard Pocket Duo sits in an interesting position among them. It's considerably more capable than Retroid's entry-level offering, but it doesn't have the outright processing power of some of the more expensive competition. At this price, I think it's fair to expect more than simply being able to run DS/3DS games nicely. I want to know whether Retroid has found a sensible balance between power, portability, comfort and those two rather beautiful screens.

Some comparisons pictures of the Retroid Pocket Duo (the light gray colored handheld here) with the AYN Thor (Black) and Anbernic's RG DS Plus (Coral Pink)

Something else I've become increasingly interested in is the software being developed around these handhelds, because having two physical displays is only part of what makes them interesting. The other part, and arguably the more important one, is what people decide to do with them. For this review, I've been chatting with several developers whose projects approach dual-screen gaming from very different directions. items.title: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
items.content:
Security personnel around the world are on high alert Tuesday following the discovery of eight TLS certificates with private keys so weak they could allow anyone to mint trusted browser and app credentials for any site on the Internet.

As of late morning Tuesday, browser makers and some major apps and programming languages had blocked all eight of the intermediate certificates. There are no reports of certificate transparency logs, which track the issuance of all browser-trusted certificates, showing the compromised keys being used maliciously. The threat remains far from over, however, because it will be hard and time-consuming to update other key parts of the Internet, such as Linux distributions and embedded and Internet of Things devices.

The eight intermediate certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited. An informal advisory published to emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com over on Tuesday posted the message “We have a problem here – Wayne.” The words were digitally signed using the private key of one of the eMudhra certificates. With proof that the reporting party had control of the key, defenders scrambled because the same key could be used to sign unauthorized certificates that would be trusted by millions of servers worldwide.

“This will be a massive cleanup job, bigger than Heartbleed,” Filippo Valsorda, a cryptography engineer and a cryptography maintainer for the open source Go programming language, told Ars. “There will be a very, very long tail, IoT devices, Docker containers, forgotten Linux machines, unmaintained CLI tools that shipped their own copy of the roots (which is common in some ecosystems, like Python). Also, Linux distributions are still rolling out updates, some of them are not ready yet, and then system administrators will need to apply them to a lot of machines.”

Heartbleed is the name of a critical vulnerability in the OpenSSL cryptography library. In 2014, it came under mass exploitation . Exploits let many unaffiliated hackers decrypt TLS-protected exchanges between parties. They also recovered private TLS certificate keys, session cookies, and passwords. The attacks compromised thousands of servers, some belonging to large companies and government agencies around the world.

Recovery required a long series of steps that took years. Steps included patching OpenSSL on all affected devices, reissuing millions of TLS keys, revoking old certificates, rotating passwords and session tokens and updating embedded devices and other forgotten systems—something that was extremely time- and resource-intensive, especially at Internet scale.

“Every time you need a lot of different people in different contexts to do something, it will take a long time,” Valsorda explained. “This time it’s worse because there’s more contexts, more people, and more heterogeneity.”

The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2 384 , or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

“That is extremely in the ‘this should not be possible’ category,” Valdorda said. “Maybe some horribly dangerous key generation interface has a ‘size’ parameter and they set it to 1 by mistake???”

Ben Cartwright-Cox, director of BGP.tools, said: “My guess is that it’s example code that accidentally leaked to production, but hard to know. But it’s bonkers that no one noticed.”

items.title: What requirements don't you have?
items.content:
When designing software, the requirements you don’t have are as important as the requirements you do. Identifying what you can compromise on — what can be slow, or stale, or inflexible — is usually the key to an elegant design.

For instance, take preforking web servers like Unicorn . Because they lack the feature of shared mutable state between server instances, they can run each server in its own process, which provides isolation for free. Because Unicorn specifically ignores the problem of slow client handling 1 , it can queue requests directly on Unix sockets, drastically simplifying the implementation.

Because S3 does not support atomic multi-key updates — you cannot update multiple blobs in a single transaction — it can store data at the blob level however it chooses. That makes it much faster, since reads and writes don’t have to cross storage partitions, and much easier to scale, since less coordination means fewer sources of truth.

StatsD uses UDP by default, which means it doesn’t guarantee that every piece of data you send makes it into storage. In exchange for dropping that requirement, it incurs much less network overhead, which is a big advantage for a stats aggregation service that’s constantly shoveling data over the wire.

The general design approach of fanning out data to an edge cache buys a lot of speed and scaling by dropping the requirement that data must always be up-to-date. SQLite buys operational simplicity — it can run out of a single file! — by dropping the requirement of concurrent writes. By accepting high tail latency 2 , Cursor can scale their distributed git backend more easily. Well-designed systems turn their weaknesses into strengths.

Anyone who’s spent time designing real-world software (or who’s studied distributed systems ) knows that system design is a process of compromise. If you attempt to satisfy every single potential requirement — speed, concurrency, up-to-date data, a simple interface, supporting complex user behaviors — you will fail to design a working system at all.

Figuring out what requirements you can relax is difficult because it combines both business and technical expertise . It is technically challenging to identify precisely the level of staleness that a particular design change will allow; it is likewise challenging from a business perspective to determine whether that level of staleness is acceptable to users.

In most cases, an engineer who understands the technical side must try and explain it to a product manager, who can make a judgement on the business side. But this is a very difficult partnership to get right. Engineers and PMs have different incentives and little ability to check each other’s work, which makes it hard to build trust . Without trust, the product manager is liable to avoid giving any ground at all 3 , which leaves the design in an impossible state.

This is an underappreciated reason why solo developers or startups can sometimes run rings around larger companies. Because the technical and business decisions are united in a single person, they can make design tradeoffs that would be impossible for a large company, enabling them to build systems that are far more elegant and powerful.

Knowing what requirements you don’t have becomes far more important when working with coding agents. Frontier models are very capable, but they have all gone through the purifying flames of RLVR : like high-achieving schoolchildren, they are obsessed with satisfying the Grader. On top of that, they have very little business context compared to an experienced human. That often manifests as them catching correctness or consistency “bugs” that are really just hypothetical unsatisfied requirements.

For instance, it’s not uncommon for an LLM to casually introduce a mutex or other concurrency mechanism to ensure that two pieces of semi-related data are kept in sync, even if not told to do so. I’ve seen LLMs add weird checks in the middle of request handling to…

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Microsoft reportedly projects $1,200 to $1,800 price for 2028 Project Helix
items.content:
We haven’t heard many details about Microsoft’s upcoming “Project Helix” gaming hardware since the company announced it in March as a device that will “play your Xbox and PC games.” In a new wide-ranging profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma , though, Fortune alludes to a dual release strategy for upcoming Microsoft gaming hardware, with “a next-generation handheld device” planned by the end of next year and a 2028 holiday season console release that could cost between $1,200 and $1,800.

That future console price range is based on what has “internally been projected” at the company, according to Fortune. But the price for consumers could come down if “Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost,” the outlet says, as many console makers have done in the past .

While a $1,200 starting price would be historically high for the game console market, even accounting for inflation , it also reflects a new normal: The slowdown in Moore’s Law and AI-driven component shortages mean cutting-edge gaming hardware just isn’t as cheap as it used to be. This year, the Steam Machine broke the $1,000 starting price , while the 2-year-old technology in the PlayStation 5 Pro is now going for $900 , and the 6-year-old Xbox Series X now starts at $750 .

Fortune also reports that Microsoft is beset by internal clashes over whether its upcoming Helix handheld will run a “trimmed-down version of Windows Home”—akin to last year’s ROG Xbox Ally —or a bespoke operating system built and controlled by the Xbox group. Fortune cites “people briefed on the clash” in reporting that one high-level executive threatened to cancel the handheld altogether if they were forced to use Windows.

That threat seemingly helped lead to the current situation with the Xbox team “now largely controlling the direction of the operating system for the project, Fortune writes, though Sharma said the two groups are still working closely together. Fortune also reports that Microsoft has pressured the hardware team to move up the timelines for Project Helix hardware “by at least several months,” in part by using AI tools where applicable.

The profile also cites “people familiar with the strategy” in reporting that Xbox Game Pass will soon shift to a heavily tiered “a la carte” structure that lets subscribers pick and choose “add-ons for console-only games, cloud gaming, and multiplayer.” That would be an interesting shift from the current Game Pass plans, which all include some level of cloud-based gaming, console exclusives, and console multiplayer even for players who don’t make use of them.

Elsewhere in the wide-ranging profile, Fortune addresses concerns from “several current and former staff members” that Sharma was put in place merely to enact painful cuts before an impending sale of a spinoff of the Xbox group. But the piece also quotes Microsoft executive Judson Althoff pushing back against that idea, saying, “We would not have put [Sharma] on a business we intend to sell. There’s going to be a ton of speculation about all this. Time will tell.”

Kyle Orland has been the Senior Gaming Editor at Ars Technica since 2012, writing primarily about the business, tech, and culture behind video games. He has journalism and computer science degrees from University of Maryland. He once wrote a whole book about Minesweeper .

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다
